swapped.why: The Bible gives only one fact about Shadrach alone (his new name in place of Hananiah), and everything else he did and suffered is shared with Meshach and Abednego, so there are not 7 different facts that point to him alone.

Nearly every BSB fact about Meshach is shared with Shadrach and Abednego, and the only facts that tell him apart (his Hebrew name Mishael, or being named between the other two) would each give the word away alone, so the 7 clues cannot point to him without one giving him away.
Apart from his Hebrew name Azariah, every BSB fact about Abednego is shared with Shadrach and Meshach, so seven clues cannot fit only this word.

Beyond his call at the tax booth and the meal at his house, the Bible gives too few distinct facts about Matthew: leaving everything, being son of Alphaeus, and his banquet only restate those two scenes, and his other mentions just list him among the twelve.
The BSB names Luke in only three verses, which give just a few facts (beloved physician, Paul's fellow worker who sent greetings, and the only one still with Paul), not enough for 7 different clues.
Rhoda appears only in one short scene in Acts 12, so the BSB does not give 7 truly different facts about her.

The BSB names Ur of the Chaldeans in only four passages, and they give just three facts: Haran died there, Terah's family left it for Canaan, and God brought Abram out of it. That is not enough for 7 different clues.

Gomorrah is almost never mentioned apart from Sodom, so only two small details (King Birsha and the Ammonites comparison) set it apart, and the Bible does not give 7 different facts that point to it rather than to Sodom.

The BSB names Ararat in only three distinct settings (the ark's resting place, the refuge of Sennacherib's assassins told twice in matching verses, and a kingdom summoned against Babylon), which is not enough for 7 different facts.

Golgotha appears only in the crucifixion account, so the Bible gives no seven different facts about it that avoid naming or pointing straight to the crucifixion, and every clue would give the word away on Monday.

The BSB names Tarsus in only five verses, and they give about five different facts (Saul's hometown, in Cilicia, 'no ordinary city', Saul sent there, Barnabas sought him there), which is not enough for 7 different clues.
Patmos is named only once in the Bible (Revelation 1:9), so the BSB gives just one fact about the island itself, and any other clues would describe John's vision rather than the place.

The Bible describes the ladder in a single verse, which gives only about four facts about it (it rests on the earth, its top reaches heaven, angels go up and down it, the LORD stands at its top), so the other clues would describe Jacob's journey or God's promises instead of the ladder.
The jawbone appears only in Judges 15:15-17, so the Bible does not give 7 different facts about it, and the clues would keep repeating the same few verses.

The BSB uses fleece in only three places (Gideon's dew test, Job 31:20 and Deuteronomy 18:4), so at least five of the seven clues must come from the five verses of the Gideon test, and almost any one of those gives the word away, leaving too few distinct medium-hard facts.
The BSB mentions mustard only in the single mustard seed parable and the one 'faith the size of a mustard seed' saying, which is too little for 7 different facts.

The BSB gives only about five distinct facts about the manger (Job's wild ox, Proverbs' empty manger, Isaiah's donkey, and the Luke 2 birth, sign and shepherds), and the three Luke verses largely repeat one another, so seven different clues aren't possible.

"Coin" is a general noun for many different coins in the Bible (the four-drachma coin in the fish, the denarius, the lost silver coin, the widow's copper coins, Judas's thirty pieces), so no single thing fits it, and the only single-coin word that would fit, "denarius", has too few distinct BSB facts of its own for seven clues.
The BSB passages on sparrows are one teaching told twice (cheaply sold, never forgotten by God, you are worth more), which gives far fewer than 7 different facts.

In the BSB the lyre appears almost only in lists beside the harp, horn, flute and tambourine, so there aren't 7 distinct facts to build clues from, and nearly every clue would fit 'harp' just as well.
The BSB mentions lentils in only four passages (Genesis 25, 2 Samuel 17, 2 Samuel 23 and Ezekiel 4), which is not enough for 7 different facts.

The BSB gives only about four distinct facts about the rooster (its strut in Proverbs, the 'when the rooster crows' watch hour, Jesus' warning to Peter, and its crowing at Peter's denial), too few for seven different clues.

The BSB uses "exodus" only once (Hebrews 11:22, where Joseph speaks of it near his death), and the other supplied verses are about Isaac, Jacob and Moses' early life rather than the exodus, so there aren't 7 different facts about the word to clue.
The BSB uses this word only in the triumphal entry shout and the children's temple shout, which is too few distinct facts for 7 clues.
The BSB uses 'Messiah' in only four verses (Daniel 9:25, 9:26, John 1:41, 4:25), which is not enough for 7 different facts, and the John clues fit 'Christ' just as well.

Abba appears only three times in the BSB, and two of them (Romans and Galatians) say nearly the same thing about the Spirit of adoption crying out, so there aren't 7 different facts about the word itself.
The BSB names Ebenezer in only three verses (1 Samuel 4:1, 5:1, 7:12), which is not enough for 7 different facts about the word itself without stretching the surrounding battle story.
The Bible gives no fact that sets Sheol apart from 'the grave', 'hell', 'the pit' or 'death', since those verses use those words in other translations, so no set of clues can fit only this word.

clues.text: In Eden, he gave names to all the livestock, the birds of the air, and every beast of the field.
The LORD God caused him to fall into a deep sleep, took one of his ribs, and closed up the flesh.
After he ate from the forbidden tree, God told him the ground was cursed and he would toil.
In the earliest record of generations, he lived a total of 930 years and then died.
God drove him out of Eden and placed cherubim with a flaming sword to guard the tree of life.
Writing to Corinth, Paul says that as in him all die, so in Christ all will be made alive.
Enoch, who prophesied the Lord coming with myriads of holy ones, is called the seventh from him.
In Eden, God told her He would sharply increase her pain in childbirth.
She named a son Seth, saying God had granted her another seed in place of the one Cain killed.
She later gave birth to Cain's brother, who was a keeper of sheep.
Writing to Timothy, Paul said the man was formed first, and then she was formed.
Paul feared the Corinthians might be led astray, just as she was deceived by the serpent's cunning.
She told the serpent God had said not to eat or touch the fruit of the tree in the middle of the garden.
After the forbidden fruit was eaten, the LORD God made garments of skin and clothed her and her husband.
When the LORD asked him where his brother was, he answered that he did not know.
This tiller of the soil brought fruit of the ground to the LORD, but God had no regard for his offering.
He asked his brother to go out to the field, and there he rose up and killed him.
When this son of Adam grew angry, the LORD warned him that sin was crouching at his door.
The LORD placed a mark on this son of Adam so that no one who found him would kill him.
Told by the LORD he would be a fugitive and a wanderer, he said his punishment was more than he could bear.
Jude warns of false teachers who have traveled this man's path, alongside Balaam's error and Korah's rebellion.
Eve's younger son, he was a keeper of sheep while his older brother worked the soil.
He brought the LORD the best portions of the firstborn of his flock, and God looked on him with favor.
His brother invited him out to the field, then rose up against him there and killed him.
A New Testament roll of the faithful says he was commended as righteous and by faith still speaks though dead.
The New Testament says Jesus' sprinkled blood, as mediator of a new covenant, speaks a better word than this man's blood.
Eve named her son Seth, saying God had granted her another seed in place of this murdered son.
Jesus warned the scribes and Pharisees about the righteous blood shed on earth, from his blood to Zechariah's.
Before the flood, this man walked with God, and then he was no more, because God took him away.
Among the long-lived men in the family line from Adam, he lived a total of 365 years.
In the generations after Adam, at age sixty-five he became the father of Methuselah.
In the line of Seth, Jared was 162 years old when he became this man's father.
In the list of faithful people of old, he was commended as one who pleased God.
Called the seventh from Adam, he prophesied that the Lord would come with myriads of His holy ones.
In the family line from Adam to Noah, this man was Noah's great-grandfather.
Waiting for the waters to go down, he sent out a bird that came back at evening with a freshly plucked leaf.
After the great flood, this man of the soil planted a vineyard and became drunk in his tent.
His father Lamech named him, hoping this son would bring comfort from toil on the ground the LORD had cursed.
He became a father after he was 500 years old and lived 950 years in all.
Ezekiel names him with Daniel and Job as righteous men whose righteousness could save only themselves.
Stepping onto dry land after a long voyage, he built an altar and offered clean animals and birds to the LORD.
Peter calls him a preacher of righteousness, kept safe among eight people when God judged the ancient world.
On the day the floodwaters came, this son of Noah entered the ark with his brothers and their wives.
After Noah drank wine and lay uncovered in his tent, this son and Japheth walked backward to cover their father.
Noah said, "Blessed be the LORD, the God of" this son, and declared that Canaan would be his servant.
This older brother of Japheth was the forefather of all the sons of Eber.
Two years after the flood, at 100 years old, this man became the father of Arphaxad.
In the list of clans after the flood, Elam, Asshur, Lud and Aram are named among this man's sons.
In one family line, this man's descendants run down through Peleg, Nahor and Terah to Abram.
On a mountain, he saw a ram caught by its horns in a thicket and offered it in place of his son.
Sitting at his tent entrance by the Oaks of Mamre, he ran to meet three men and bowed low.
Pleading with the LORD over Sodom, he asked again and again until God agreed to spare it for ten righteous people.
God gave him a new name, saying He had made him a father of many nations.
He was a hundred years old when his long-awaited son was finally born to him.
Melchizedek, king of Salem, met him returning from the slaughter of the kings and blessed him.
In a story Jesus told, a rich man in Hades looked up and saw him far off, with Lazarus by his side.
Worn out and with her master old, she laughed to herself at the thought of having this pleasure.
God promised she would become the mother of nations, and that kings of peoples would descend from her.
The king of Gerar gave her brother a thousand pieces of silver as her vindication, declaring her completely cleared.
She told Abraham to drive out Hagar and her son, so that boy would not share the inheritance.
By faith, though barren and past the proper age, she was enabled to conceive because she trusted the One who promised.
She died at Kiriath-arba, the town also called Hebron, in the land of Canaan.
Peter told wives they are her children if they do what is right and refuse to give way to fear.
After ten years in Canaan, Abram's childless wife gave him her Egyptian maidservant to be his wife.
Once she knew she was pregnant by Abram, this servant began to despise her mistress.
Fleeing harsh treatment, she was found by the angel of the LORD at a desert spring on the road to Shur.
After an angel spoke to her by a spring, she called the LORD "the God who sees me."
Early one morning Abraham put bread and a skin of water on her shoulders and sent her away with a boy.
In the Wilderness of Beersheba, she sat a bowshot away from her boy and wept as their water ran out.
Paul wrote that this slave woman stands for Mount Sinai in Arabia and the present-day Jerusalem.
The angel of the LORD said this unborn boy would be a wild donkey of a man, his hand against everyone.
God promised Abraham that this son would become the father of twelve rulers and a great nation.
He was thirteen years old when he was circumcised along with his father Abraham's household.
Sarah saw her husband Abraham's son by another woman mocking her own son.
Abraham sent him and his mother away with bread and a skin of water, and she wandered in the Wilderness of Beersheba.
He and his half brother Isaac buried their father Abraham in the cave of Machpelah.
When Hagar ran from Sarai, an angel told her to name her unborn son because the LORD heard her cry.
When the LORD rained sulfur and fire on Sodom, his wife looked back and became a pillar of salt.
After his herdsmen quarreled with Abram's herdsmen, he chose the well-watered plain of the Jordan for himself.
Four kings carried him off from Sodom, and Abram chased them with 318 trained men to rescue him.
Sitting in the gateway of Sodom, he welcomed two angels into his house and baked them unleavened bread.
Told by angels to flee Sodom to the mountains, he begged to escape to a small nearby town instead.
His two daughters bore sons named Moab and Ben-ammi, fathers of the Moabites and the Ammonites.
Peter calls him a righteous man, tormented by the lawless deeds he saw while living in Sodom.
On a mountain in the land of Moriah, his father bound him and laid him on the altar atop the wood.
Walking up the mountain with his father, he asked where the lamb for the burnt offering was.
Abraham held a great feast on the day this child was weaned.
Meditating in a field one evening, he looked up and saw camels bringing his future bride.
Old and unable to see, he touched his son's hairy hands and said the voice did not match them.
After the herdsmen of Gerar quarreled over his wells, he dug another and named it Rehoboth.
At Gerar, the king of the Philistines looked down from a window and saw him caressing his wife.
At a spring, she gave Abraham's servant a drink and then drew water for all his camels.
Her family asked if she would leave with Abraham's servant, and she answered, "I will go."
Seeing Isaac in the field as the camels arrived, she took her veil and covered herself.
When twins struggled inside her, the LORD told her that two nations were in her womb.
Isaac loved Esau because he liked wild game, but this mother loved Jacob.
She put young goat skins on Jacob's hands and neck so blind Isaac would bless him.
In Gerar, Isaac called his wife his sister, until King Abimelech saw him caressing her.
At his birth he came out red, covered with hair like a fur coat, and he was named for it.
After eating his brother's bread and lentil stew, he got up and went away, despising his birthright.
When the boys grew up, he became a skillful hunter, a man of the field, while his brother stayed home.
His father told him he would live by the sword and serve his brother, but one day tear off his yoke.
Holding a grudge over a stolen blessing, he planned to kill his brother once their father's days of mourning came.
As his returning brother bowed to the ground seven times, he ran to him, embraced and kissed him, and both wept.
He took his wives, children, livestock and all he had gained in Canaan and moved far away from his brother.
Isaac's younger twin was born holding on to his brother's heel.
He gave his brother Esau bread and lentil stew, and Esau ate, left, and despised his birthright.
His blind father touched him and said the voice was his, but the hands were Esau's.
Traveling from Beersheba toward Haran, he dreamed of a ladder to heaven with God's angels going up and down.
He served his uncle Laban seven years for Rachel, and it seemed like only a few days.
Wrestling a man until daybreak, he refused to let go unless the man blessed him.
Brought by Joseph before Pharaoh in Egypt, he said his travels had lasted 130 years.
At a well near Haran, Jacob rolled the stone away and watered the sheep this shepherdess brought.
Jacob served Laban seven years for her, and it seemed but a few days because of his love.
After Jacob's wedding feast, Laban gave him her older sister Leah instead, and Jacob found out in the morning.
After years without children, Jacob's wife named her first son Joseph and asked the LORD for another son.
When Laban searched her tent, she sat on his stolen household idols hidden in her camel's saddlebag.
With her last breath, she named her newborn son Ben-oni, but Jacob called the boy Benjamin.
After Herod killed the boys of Bethlehem, Matthew recalled a voice in Ramah: she weeps for her children.
Laban's older daughter, described as having weak eyes, while her younger sister was shapely and beautiful.
On Jacob's wedding night, Laban secretly gave her to him instead of the bride he had worked seven years for.
She named her fourth son Judah, saying, "This time I will praise the LORD."
In Paddan-aram, she let Rachel have her son's mandrakes in exchange for a night with Jacob.
When she stopped bearing children, this wife of Jacob gave her maidservant Zilpah to him as a wife.
She was the mother of Dinah, the daughter of Jacob who was taken by Shechem son of Hamor.
Jacob buried her in the cave of Machpelah, where Abraham, Sarah, Isaac and Rebekah were also buried.
In Egypt, he asked his brothers to come near and told them he was the brother they had sold.
He told his brothers a dream in which the sun, moon and eleven stars bowed down to him.
His brothers pulled him out of a pit and sold him to Ishmaelites for twenty shekels of silver.
In Egypt, his master's wife grabbed his cloak, but he left it in her hand and ran outside.
Israel loved this son born in his old age more than the others and made him a robe of many colors.
Pharaoh put his own signet ring on this man's finger and a gold chain around his neck.
Standing before Pharaoh, he said the king's dreams were one and the same, showing what God was about to do.
With her last breath, the dying Rachel gave this son one name, but his father called him another.
During the famine, Jacob would not send this son to Egypt with his brothers, fearing harm.
At Joseph's meal in Egypt, this brother's portion was five times larger than anyone else's.
Joseph's steward searched the brothers' sacks and found the silver cup in this youngest brother's sack.
In Jacob's last blessings to his sons, this son is called a ravenous wolf that devours prey.
Saul told Samuel he came from this tribe, the smallest tribe of Israel.
Paul wrote that he was circumcised on the eighth day and belonged to this tribe of Israel.
After his birth, Leah said, "This time I will praise the LORD," and then she stopped having children.
When his brothers planned to kill Joseph, this brother asked what profit they would gain from covering up his blood.
Told that his daughter-in-law Tamar was pregnant, this son of Jacob ordered her brought out and burned to death.
He urged his father Israel, "Send the boy with me," so the family might live and not die.
In Egypt, this brother approached Joseph and begged him not to be angry, saying he was equal to Pharaoh himself.
Jacob called this son a young lion who crouches, and like a lioness no one dares rouse him.
Jacob said the scepter would not depart from this son, nor the staff from between his feet.
When Moses asked him to let Israel go, he replied, "Who is the LORD that I should obey His voice?"
Though Moses and Aaron did many wonders before him, the LORD hardened his heart so he would not let Israel go.
When Aaron's staff became a serpent before him, he called his magicians, who did the same by their magic arts.
During the plague of frogs, he begged Moses and Aaron to pray and promised to let Israel go.
Summoning Moses and Aaron during the plagues on Egypt, he admitted, "This time I have sinned. The LORD is righteous."
At midnight the LORD struck down every firstborn in Egypt, even the firstborn of this king on his throne.
His entire army of chariots and horsemen chased the Israelites into the sea, and not one of them survived.
The angel of the LORD appeared to him in a blazing fire within a bush, yet the bush was not consumed.
This leader of Israel died at a hundred and twenty, yet his eyes were not weak and his vitality had not diminished.
He stretched out his hand over the sea at daybreak, and the waters returned upon the fleeing Egyptians.
God told him to chisel out two new stone tablets to replace the first ones, which he had broken.
The Israelites saw that his face was radiant after speaking with the LORD, so he covered it with a veil.
During the battle with Amalek, Aaron and Hur held up his tired hands until the sun went down.
Before the disciples, he and Elijah suddenly appeared on a mountain, talking with Jesus.
As the people waited for Moses to come down the mountain, this leader told them to bring him their gold earrings.
Before Pharaoh, his staff became a serpent and swallowed up the staffs the others threw down.
In the Tent of the Testimony, his staff for the house of Levi sprouted, blossomed and produced almonds.
As Joshua fought the Amalekites, he and Hur held up Moses' tired hands until sunset.
In the wilderness, he and Miriam criticized Moses because of the Cushite woman Moses had married.
On Mount Hor his priestly garments were put on his son Eleazar, and he died there.
When a plague broke out after Korah's rebellion, he ran among the people with incense and made atonement.
After Israel crossed the sea, a prophetess took a tambourine, and all the women followed her with dancing.
Beside the sea she sang, "Sing to the LORD, for He is highly exalted; the horse and rider He has thrown into the sea."
In the wilderness, she and Aaron criticized Moses because of the Cushite woman he had married.
As the cloud lifted from the Tent of Meeting, she suddenly became leprous, white as snow.
While Israel stayed at Kadesh in the Wilderness of Zin, she died and was buried there.
In the wilderness she was confined outside the camp seven days, and the people did not move on until she returned.
Israel was told to remember what the LORD their God did to her on the journey after leaving Egypt.
Moses was tending this man's flock on the far side of the wilderness when he came to Horeb.
This priest of Midian heard how the LORD had brought Israel out of Egypt.
When Moses asked to go back to his brothers in Egypt, this man told him, "Go in peace."
After Moses sent his wife Zipporah back, this man received her.
Visiting Moses' camp in the desert, he declared that the LORD is greater than all other gods.
He brought a burnt offering to God, and Aaron and Israel's elders ate bread with him.
He saw Moses judging the people alone from morning till evening and asked him why.
After Moses agreed to stay with Reuel in Midian, Reuel gave Moses this daughter as his wife.
She bore Moses a son, Gershom, named because Moses had become a foreigner in a foreign land.
When the LORD met Moses at a lodging place and was about to kill him, she grabbed a flint knife.
After circumcising her son, she said to Moses, 'Surely you are a bridegroom of blood to me.'
Moses sent her back, and his father-in-law Jethro, the priest of Midian, took her in.
She was mother of Eliezer, named because God delivered Moses from the sword of Pharaoh.
Jethro brought her and her sons to Moses, camped in the desert at the mountain of God.
He told Balak's servants that not even a house full of silver and gold could make him defy the LORD.
The angel of the LORD stood in his road with a drawn sword, and his donkey turned off into a field.
The king of Moab sent messengers to summon him from Pethor, by the Euphrates in the land of his people.
Before seeking the LORD, he told the king of Moab to build seven altars and prepare seven bulls and seven rams.
Hired to curse Israel, he blessed them three times, and the king of Moab struck his hands together in anger.
Looking over Israel's camp, this diviner foretold that a star will come forth from Jacob and a scepter from Israel.
When Israel waged war against Midian and killed its five kings, this son of Beor was also killed with the sword.
After the priests circled Jericho the seventh time and blew their horns, he commanded the people to shout.
On the day the LORD gave the Amorites to Israel, he called for the sun to stand still over Gibeon.
Of the men Moses sent to spy out the land, only he and Caleb son of Jephunneh stayed alive.
Moses told him to choose men and fight the Amalekites while Moses stood on the hilltop with God's staff.
Near Jericho he met the Commander of the LORD's army and was told to take off his sandals.
At Gilgal he set up the twelve stones the Israelites had carried out of the Jordan.
As Moses' young assistant, he would not leave the tent where the LORD spoke with Moses face to face.
After the spies returned to Moses, he quieted the people and said Israel could certainly conquer the land.
God said this servant had a different spirit and followed Him wholeheartedly, so he would enter the promised land.
He recalled being forty years old when Moses sent him from Kadesh-barnea to spy out the land.
Speaking to Joshua, he said he was still as strong for war as on the day Moses sent him out.
Joshua blessed this man and gave him Hebron as his inheritance.
He drove the three sons of Anak, Sheshai, Ahiman and Talmai, out of Hebron.
He offered his daughter Acsah in marriage to the man who struck down and captured Kiriath-sepher.
When the king of Jericho demanded the Israelite spies, she claimed they had left at dusk as the gate closed.
In Jericho, she hid two of Joshua's spies on her roof among stalks of flax laid out there.
Her house was built into the wall of Jericho, so she let two spies down by a rope through a window.
Two Israelite spies told her to tie a scarlet cord in her window and gather her whole family inside.
After Jericho's wall collapsed, the young spies brought her and her family out and settled them outside Israel's camp.
In the family line of Jesus, Salmon was the father of Boaz by this woman.
A New Testament letter says she was justified by her actions when she welcomed the spies and sent them off another route.
Married to a man named Lappidoth, she was a prophetess in Israel.
She sat under a palm tree between Ramah and Bethel, and the Israelites came to her for judgment.
She summoned Barak and told him to march to Mount Tabor with ten thousand men of Naphtali and Zebulun.
When Barak would not go to battle without her, she went but said a woman would get Sisera.
At Mount Tabor she told Barak to arise, for the LORD had delivered Sisera into his hand that day.
After Sisera's army fell, she and Barak son of Abinoam sang a song to the LORD together.
In a victory song she called herself a mother in Israel, rising when life in the villages had ceased.
Deborah summoned this son of Abinoam from Kedesh and told him to march to Mount Tabor.
Called to fight Sisera, he said he would go only if Deborah the prophetess went with him.
Deborah warned this commander the honor would not be his, because the LORD would hand Sisera to a woman.
He chased Sisera's chariots and army to Harosheth-hagoyim, and not a single enemy soldier was left.
Arriving in pursuit of Sisera, he was led into Jael's tent and found the enemy commander dead.
On the day Jabin's army was beaten, he and Deborah sang a song of praise to the LORD.
In a list of the heroes of faith, he is named right after Gideon and just before Samson.
Deborah's song names her beside Shamgar son of Anath, in days when Israel's highways were deserted.
Sisera fled on foot to her tent, because her husband Heber's house was at peace with Jabin king of Hazor.
She went out to meet the fleeing Sisera, told him not to be afraid, and covered him with a blanket.
When Sisera asked her for a little water, she opened a container of milk and gave him a drink.
While Sisera slept from exhaustion, she took a hammer and drove a tent peg through his temple.
When Barak came chasing Sisera, she went out and offered to show him the man he was seeking.
In the song of Deborah and Barak, this wife of Heber the Kenite is called most blessed among women.
He commanded the army of Jabin king of Canaan and lived in Harosheth-hagoyim.
Told that Barak had gone up Mount Tabor, he called out nine hundred iron chariots to the River Kishon.
When the LORD routed his army before Barak, he abandoned his chariot and fled on foot.
Resting in Jael's tent, he asked for a little water, and she gave him milk instead.
As he lay sleeping from exhaustion, Jael drove a tent peg through his temple into the ground.
His mother peered through the lattice, asking why his chariot was so long in coming.
In the song of Deborah and Barak, the stars fought against him from their courses.
The angel of the LORD found him threshing wheat in a winepress, hiding it from the Midianites.
Asking God for a sign, he laid a wool fleece on the threshing floor and asked for dew on it alone.
The LORD told him to keep only the three hundred men who lapped the water and send the others home.
His three companies blew rams' horns, shattered their jars, and held up torches to rout the Midianites.
One night the LORD told him to tear down his father's altar to Baal and cut down the Asherah pole.
When Israel asked him and his son to rule over them, he refused and said the LORD would rule.
From plundered gold he made an ephod in his hometown of Ophrah, and it became a snare to his household.
His father Gilead's other sons drove him out, saying he was the son of another woman.
After fleeing his brothers to the land of Tob, this man of Gilead gathered worthless men around him.
When the Ammonites made war on Israel, the elders of Gilead came asking this man to be their commander.
Before fighting the Ammonites, he vowed a burnt offering of whatever came out his door to greet him.
Returning victorious to Mizpah, this judge saw his only child, a daughter, coming out with tambourines and dancing.
Under this judge, Gileadites at the Jordan fords killed any Ephraimite who said Sibboleth instead of Shibboleth.
A New Testament roll of the faithful names him alongside Gideon, Barak, Samson, David and Samuel.
In the Valley of Sorek, a woman lulled him to sleep on her lap and had his seven braids shaved off.
Near the vineyards of Timnah, the Spirit of the LORD came on him and he tore apart a roaring young lion.
At Lehi the ropes fell from his arms, and he struck down a thousand Philistines with a donkey's jawbone.
Bracing against two central pillars, he pushed with all his might and brought a Philistine temple down on its lords.
He tied torches between the tails of three hundred foxes and burned the Philistines' standing grain.
At midnight in Gaza, he pulled up the city gate doors and posts and carried them toward Hebron.
During a seven-day feast, he bet thirty linen garments on a riddle about something sweet coming out of the strong.
While men hid in her room, she tied her lover with new ropes, but he snapped them like threads.
Each of the Philistine lords promised her eleven hundred shekels of silver if she would entice a man.
In the time of the judges, a man from Israel fell in love with her in the Valley of Sorek.
While a man slept, she wove the seven braids of his hair into the web of a loom.
After lulling a man to sleep on her lap, she called for someone to shave off his seven braids.
